straight/data: Here are two classes, each point placed by two features, x zero and x one. Class one fills a vee, and class zero wraps around it.
straight/line: A linear classifier draws one straight border. Turn it and slide it however you like: some points always land on the wrong side.
straight/book: In 1969, Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert's book, Perceptrons, mapped out limits like this one: many patterns are out of reach when the inputs feed straight into the outputs.
straight/fix: They also pointed out the way around it: a layer of units in between, which recodes the input before anything is scored.
lines/n0: So put a layer in between. Its first unit is a neuron, which draws a line: silent on one side, and rising with the distance on the other.
lines/n1: A second neuron draws its own line, tilted the other way.
lines/layer: Neurons side by side, reading the same input, form a layer. Their outputs make a vector, h, one number per neuron.
lines/hidden: In their 1986 backprop paper, Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams call such units hidden: they are part of neither the input nor the output. The data never shows their values.
lines/score: On top sits a linear classifier that scores h instead of x. Class zero's score adds the two outputs: zero inside the vee, where both neurons are silent, and growing outside it.
lines/one: Class one's score is one, minus that same sum, so it is highest inside the vee.
lines/bent: The border sits where the two scores tie. It is made of straight pieces, yet it bends around the vee, and splits what no single line could.
numbers/x: Now in numbers. Take the point x with entries two and one, out on the right arm, where class zero lives.
numbers/W1: The hidden neurons' weights are the rows of a matrix, W one: one row per hidden unit.
numbers/z0: Unit zero dots its row with x, and adds its bias from b one: two, minus one, plus one, is two.
numbers/z1: Unit one: minus two, minus one, plus one, is minus two.
numbers/h: The ReLU keeps the two, and turns the minus two into zero. So h is two and zero: h is the ReLU of W one x, plus b one.
numbers/W2: The second layer scores h with its own weights, W two: one row per class.
numbers/s0: Class zero: one times two, plus one times zero, plus a bias of zero from b two: two.
numbers/s1: Class one: minus two, plus zero, plus one, is minus one. Class zero wins, as the picture said.
numbers/forget: Skip the ReLU, and the second layer reads minus two where it read zero. Class zero now scores zero, class one scores one, and the answer flips.
collapse/D: Real inputs are bigger: an image of three thousand and seventy two numbers, say. Write D for that count, the number of input features.
collapse/H: With H hidden units, W one has a row for each unit and a column for each input: H by D. Its bias, b one, has H entries.
collapse/C: With C classes, W two has a row per class and a column per hidden unit: C by H. Its bias, b two, has C entries.
collapse/sub: Now take the ReLU out, and put the first layer inside the second: W two, times the bracket W one x plus b one, then plus b two.
collapse/mult: Multiply it out: W two W one times x, plus a constant. C by H, times H by D, is a single C by D matrix.
collapse/one: So without the bend, the two layers collapse into one linear classifier, however many hidden units there are. On the vee, the same weights give one flat border, straight through the classes.
collapse/bend: The ReLU between the layers stops the collapse. It is what lets the border bend.
